action_trace.summary: Generated 10 targeted interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (untouched file handling, Vim/Emacs parity), pain points (friction in workflows, disruptive prompts), and acceptance criteria (configuration options, behavioral expectations, organizational standards) for VSCode's dirty-file-on-creation issue.

Generated 10 structured interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic methods to elicit end-user goals (editor parity with Vim/Emacs), pain points (unwanted save prompts on untouched files), and acceptance criteria (configurable dirty-state semantics). Questions decompose the core requirement fragment addressing Issue #327076 into testable, prioritizable user needs and technical trade-offs.

Interview questions designed to elicit user goals (workflow efficiency, behavioral consistency with Vim/Emacs), pain points (unexpected save prompts on empty files), and acceptance criteria (scope, default behavior, measurement of success) using 5W1H decomposition and Socratic probing to ground requirement clarification in VSCode Issue #327076.

End users require VSCode to distinguish between file creation/opening and actual modification, preventing 'dirty' status and save prompts for untouched files—aligning with Vim/Emacs behavior and reducing workflow friction in exploratory development scenarios.

End-users report workflow friction from VSCode's 'dirty file' prompt on unmodified files, inconsistent with Vim/Emacs standards. Core expectation: only actual content modifications should trigger dirty status; untouched files should close silently. Business value: improved developer velocity and reduced interruption during exploratory coding workflows.

End-users report productivity friction from VSCode prompting to save untouched files, creating workflow interruptions absent in Vim/Emacs and complicating team onboarding. Business impact includes cumulative time waste and adoption friction. Solution requires aligning 'dirty file' semantics to only trigger after actual content modification and providing configuration to disable prompts for empty untouched files.

Clarification needed on scope of 'untouched file' detection (creation method, file type applicability), state management (workspace persistence, recent files), edge cases (metadata changes, reversion scenarios), and configuration granularity (global vs. per-context) to ensure the dirty-file behavior aligns with Vim/Emacs mental models while maintaining VSCode's workspace integrity.

Five clarification questions raised on dirty-file detection scope, creation-path distinction, configuration file handling, setting granularity, and workspace persistence semantics to resolve ambiguities in the 'untouched files should not prompt save' requirement.

End user raises six clarification questions addressing ambiguity in 'dirty file' definition (creation method vs. file type), setting scope (global vs. contextual), workspace persistence behavior for untouched files, and relationship between storage hashing and dirty-state detection. Questions aim to resolve conflicting requirement fragments and establish clear boundaries for implementation.

Core requirement validated: untouched empty files should not trigger save prompts. Refinements needed on: creation path distinctions (UI vs. CLI vs. programmatic), setting scope (global vs. per-file-type), workspace persistence semantics, and 'modification' boundary definition. Confirm whether all three file creation paths require identical behavior or differentiated logic.

Core requirement validated: VSCode should not mark newly created, empty, unmodified files as 'dirty,' eliminating unnecessary save prompts. Six refinements needed to clarify 'untouched' definition, distinguish file creation paths, set scope boundaries, and resolve terminology overlap between 'non-existent' and 'newly created' scenarios.

EndUser confirms core requirement: VSCode should not prompt to save newly created, empty, unmodified files on exit. Requires refinement on three dimensions: (1) explicit definition of 'untouched' scope, (2) differentiation of three creation paths (UI, terminal, programmatic), (3) clarification of setting scope (global vs. per-file-type) and workspace persistence behavior. Core pain point validated—eliminates workflow friction for experienced developers expecting Vim/Emacs behavior.

Consolidated 9 structured elicitation records from EndUser dialogue addressing VSCode 'dirty file' detection for newly-created, unmodified files. Core requirement confirmed: eliminate save prompts for empty, untouched files on exit (Vim/Emacs alignment). Critical clarifications required: (1) file creation path distinction (UI vs. terminal vs. programmatic), (2) 'untouched' definition scope, (3) configuration file differentiation, (4) workspace state persistence, (5) setting scope (global vs. configurable). Records follow ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 functional/non-functional/configuration structure with MoSCoW prioritization.

Eight hierarchical, prioritized user requirements synthesized from interview records and end-user feedback. Four MUST-level requirements establish core dirty file detection logic, exit behavior, file creation path distinction, and untouched file definition. Two SHOULD-level requirements clarify configuration file handling and workspace persistence. One SHOULD-level requirement aligns behavior with Vim/Emacs standards. One COULD-level requirement enables configurable per-context behavior. All items traced to interview statements and user confirmations using MoSCoW prioritization.

Eight targeted questions probe infrastructure persistence layers, security/compliance mandates, extension ecosystem compatibility, scalability trade-offs, and definitional scope. Questions apply 5W1H and iterative paraphrasing to decompose architectural, security, and operational constraints affecting the dirty-file detection feature, grounding dialogue in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 and BABOK v3 life-cycle trade-off reasoning.

Eight targeted questions probe VSCode deployer constraints: workspace persistence architecture, security/compliance mandates for configuration files, scalability of untouched-file tracking, deployment strategy (setting vs. hard change), extension ecosystem compatibility, cross-platform file-creation semantics, monitoring/telemetry needs, and operational definition of 'untouched' state. Reasoning: Infrastructure questions expose system-level dependencies; security questions identify compliance conflicts; scalability questions validate feasibility at production scale; deployment questions clarify rollout risk; ecosystem questions surface breaking changes; platform questions address portability; observability questions enable post-deployment validation; definition questions resolve implementation ambiguity.

Targeted questions probe infrastructure constraints (file persistence timing, audit requirements), security mandates (compliance for state tracking), scalability expectations (workspace state management, file list bloat), configuration semantics (differentiated handling for system vs. user files), extension ecosystem constraints (programmatic file creation), remote deployment considerations (synchronization in distributed environments), and backward compatibility (legacy workspace migration). Chain-of-Thought reasoning: decomposed 'dirty file' requirement into seven deployment-critical dimensions to surface hidden constraints before implementation.

Deployer confirms dirty-file detection shall execute client-side with origin-attributed logging (security), lazy evaluation for 10K+ files (scalability), differentiated semantics for system vs. user files (security), and optional workspace cache partitioned by workspace ID (scalability). Configuration setting 'files.excludeUntouchedFromDirty' controls behavior globally with per-filetype overrides. Exit procedure filters untouched files (empty + zero-modification events) and closes silently without prompt. Zero incremental infrastructure cost.

Deployer constraints establish client-side dirty-file detection using SHA-256 hashing with origin-attribution for three creation paths (UI/filesystem/extension). Security mandates cryptographic state signatures and audit trails. Scalability targets: 10K+ files via lazy evaluation, <50ms cache queries. Operational procedures differentiate config files (always dirty) from content files (untouched-safe). Cost-neutral via optional SQLite cache. Availability ensured through graceful degradation to conservative dirty-marking on state corruption.

Deployer response establishes client-side dirty-file detection with origin-attribution for three creation paths, optional SQLite caching (disabled by default), security logging, and O(1) scalability to 10,000+ files. Configuration via workspace-level settings; untouched files (created but unmodified) excluded from save prompts and workspace persistence per requirements MUST-001, MUST-002, SHOULD-006.

RaiseQuestionDeployer identified six critical operational context gaps: (1) 'untouched file' definition conflation across creation/opening scenarios, (2) distinct validation logic requirements for three file creation paths with divergent security implications, (3) differentiated semantics for configuration vs. user content files, (4) workspace state persistence scope ambiguity affecting cache design, (5) origin-attribution logging infrastructure feasibility, (6) storage hash scope and collision handling. Deployer requires explicit answers before infrastructure design and security validation can proceed per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 deployment checklist.

Deployer requires operational clarification on seven critical ambiguities: (1) 'untouched file' definition conflation across creation scenarios, (2) dirty-detection semantics consistency across three file-creation paths, (3) file-type differentiation for configuration files, (4) workspace persistence scope and recovery semantics, (5) storage hash invalidation trigger conditions and scope, (6) SQLite cache default-disabled scope across deployment contexts, (7) origin-attribution logging retention and sync policy. These clarifications are prerequisite to infrastructure design, security validation, and cost-performance trade-off analysis per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148.

Deployer requests five clarifications on untouched-file definition scope, file creation path semantics parity, configuration file handling, workspace persistence design, and security validation for origin-attribution—critical for infrastructure implementation and deployment strategy alignment.

Core dirty-file detection requirement validated as deployable client-side feature. Deployment requires three critical refinements: (1) explicit scope definition for 'untouched file' (created vs. opened vs. both), (2) separate validation logic confirmation for three file creation paths with origin-attribution security gate, (3) differentiated handling decision for system configuration files versus user content. Optional SQLite cache requires cost-performance trade-off analysis for large workspaces. All infrastructure decisions are non-blocking, client-side, and scalable to enterprise workspace sizes.

Deployer validation confirms core dirty-file detection is deployable as client-side state machine with no backend infrastructure required. Three refinements required: (1) distinguish file creation paths and confirm whether dirty-detection semantics differ per path, (2) explicitly define 'untouched file' scope (created-but-unopened vs. opened-but-unmodified), (3) clarify configuration file handling and workspace persistence scope to resolve potential conflicts between 'no dirty on creation' rule and persistent state tracking. Security origin-attribution and cost-performance trade-off (SQLite cache vs. in-memory LRU) require confirmation for final deployment design.

Deployer validates core dirty-file detection requirement as deployable (client-side, low cost, minimal risk) but requires explicit scope refinement on three file creation paths, 'untouched file' definition, configuration file handling, and security origin-attribution before implementation. Seven deployment readiness gates identified; recommend stakeholder review to resolve REFINE items.

Operating environment specification for vscode_2026q3 dirty-file detection feature captures client-side execution (VSCode editor process with SHA-256 hashing), optional local SQLite cache, filesystem watcher integration for three file creation paths with origin-attribution logging, and configuration scope for system versus user files. No backend infrastructure, network connectivity, or privilege escalation required. Deployment validated as in-memory state machine with LRU cache eviction strategy. Pending deployer refinement: explicit 'untouched file' binary definition and differentiated semantics confirmation across three creation paths.

Combined approach resolves deployer clarifications on 'untouched file' definition, configuration file handling, and workspace persistence while ensuring ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 traceability and quality attribute coverage (consistency, completeness, testability).
